title: Pre-Vaccination Screening: Check Contraindications Before You Inject
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Before vaccination, verify the correct patient, product, indication, age, prior reactions, pregnancy/immunocompromise status when relevant, and current illness context according to the vaccine-specific schedule and policy.
recognize: Prior severe allergic reaction to a vaccine/component and selected live-vaccine restrictions are key screening cues.
priorities: Use the current vaccine-specific screening checklist and clarify uncertain contraindications rather than guessing.
assessMonitor: Review immunization history, allergies, current medications, pregnancy status when applicable, and prior adverse events.
interventions: Delay or proceed only according to current vaccine guidance and provider/facility protocol.
medicationSafety: Do not treat all vaccines as having identical contraindications.
redFlags: History suggesting anaphylaxis to a relevant component
teaching: Explain common expected reactions and when urgent care is needed.
delegationScope: Vaccine administration authority varies by state and setting; screening interpretation must follow policy.
examTrap: Withholding every vaccine for a mild nonfebrile illness without checking current guidance.
oneLinePearl: Screen by the specific vaccine, not by blanket rules.

title: Vaccination Anaphylaxis: Be Ready Before the Dose
bottomLine: Vaccination sites must be prepared to recognize and respond to anaphylaxis. Rapid airway/breathing compromise, hypotension, or multisystem allergic symptoms after vaccination requires immediate emergency treatment and EMS escalation.
recognize: Hives alone may occur, but respiratory compromise, hypotension, or rapidly progressive multisystem symptoms are especially concerning.
priorities: Activate the emergency protocol and administer first-line treatment per standing orders/protocol.
assessMonitor: Monitor airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and symptom progression.
interventions: Position and support the patient appropriately and continue emergency monitoring until transfer/stabilization.
medicationSafety: Do not substitute antihistamines for first-line anaphylaxis treatment when systemic anaphylaxis is present.
teaching: Patients with prior severe allergies should still follow individualized vaccination guidance rather than self-excluding without review.
delegationScope: Emergency response follows facility protocol; medication authority varies by standing order and jurisdiction.
examTrap: Giving only diphenhydramine for hypotension and wheezing after vaccination.
oneLinePearl: Anaphylaxis after a vaccine is an emergency, not a routine side effect.

title: Vaccine Storage: Potency Depends on the Cold Chain
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Vaccines exposed outside manufacturer-recommended storage conditions may lose potency. Quarantine questionable product and follow the facility/state immunization program process before use.
recognize: Temperature excursion, power failure, improper placement, or monitoring-device alert can compromise storage.
priorities: Do not administer potentially compromised vaccine until product viability is determined.
assessMonitor: Review temperature logs, excursion duration, affected lots, and storage-unit function.
interventions: Label and separate affected vaccine while obtaining program/manufacturer guidance.
medicationSafety: Never discard or use excursion-affected vaccine based solely on guesswork.
teaching: Patients may need revaccination only after official determination that a dose was invalid.
delegationScope: Temperature checks may be assigned; disposition decisions require designated vaccine-management oversight.
examTrap: Using the vaccine because it still looks normal.
oneLinePearl: Vaccine potency can be lost without visible change.
sourceBasis: CDC vaccine storage and handling principles

title: Immunization Records: Verify Before Repeating
bottomLine: Use verified records and current schedules to determine what is due. Missing documentation should trigger record-retrieval efforts and schedule review rather than assumptions about immunity or completion.
recognize: Patient recall alone may be incomplete; state registries, prior records, and pharmacy records may clarify history.
priorities: Reconcile documented doses with the current age/risk-based schedule.
assessMonitor: Check dates, product type when relevant, spacing, risk conditions, and prior valid doses.
interventions: Follow catch-up guidance rather than restarting a series unless current guidance specifically requires it.
medicationSafety: Do not duplicate doses solely because records are inconvenient to obtain when verification is feasible.
redFlags: Prior serious adverse event without clarification
teaching: Encourage patients to keep accessible immunization records.
delegationScope: Record collection may be delegated; schedule interpretation requires trained licensed/authorized staff.
examTrap: Restarting every vaccine series after a long interval.
oneLinePearl: Interrupted schedules are usually continued, not automatically restarted.

title: Screening Is for Asymptomatic Patients
bottomLine: Preventive screening recommendations apply to people without concerning symptoms. New bleeding, mass, neurologic change, unexplained weight loss, or other warning symptoms require diagnostic evaluation rather than routine screening scheduling.
recognize: Symptoms change the clinical pathway from prevention to diagnosis.
priorities: Identify red-flag symptoms before applying routine screening intervals.
assessMonitor: Clarify symptoms, duration, risk factors, and prior screening history.
interventions: Escalate symptomatic patients for appropriate diagnostic evaluation.
medicationSafety: Medication changes should not be used to mask unexplained symptoms before evaluation.
teaching: Routine screening does not replace evaluation of new symptoms.
delegationScope: Screening histories may be collected by trained staff; symptom triage/escalation follows licensed scope and policy.
examTrap: Scheduling routine screening for a patient reporting alarm symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Symptoms convert screening into diagnostic care.

title: Tobacco Cessation: Ask, Support, and Connect to Treatment
bottomLine: Tobacco cessation support should be nonjudgmental and repeated. Identify readiness, reinforce evidence-based treatment options, and connect the patient with counseling and prescribed/approved therapies.
recognize: Relapse is common and does not mean treatment has failed permanently.
priorities: Ask about tobacco/nicotine use, assess willingness, and offer practical support.
assessMonitor: Track use pattern, triggers, prior quit attempts, withdrawal symptoms, and treatment response.
interventions: Use brief counseling and referral resources and reinforce the treatment plan.
medicationSafety: Cessation medications have product-specific contraindications/interactions; verify the prescribed plan.
redFlags: Severe mood change or adverse medication effects during treatment
teaching: A lapse can be used to revise the plan rather than abandon the quit attempt.
delegationScope: Education reinforcement may be shared; prescribing is outside PN scope.
oneLinePearl: Relapse calls for a revised plan, not blame.

title: Preventive Fall Review: Fix Risks Before the Fall
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Fall prevention is strongest when medication effects, vision, footwear, strength, orthostasis, environmental hazards, and assistive-device use are reviewed together.
recognize: Prior falls, dizziness, sedating medications, poor lighting, loose rugs, and weak gait increase risk.
priorities: Identify modifiable risks and reinforce individualized prevention strategies.
assessMonitor: Review fall history, gait/balance, orthostatic symptoms, medication effects, home setup, and vision/hearing.
interventions: Use safe footwear, lighting, grab supports, assistive devices, and exercise/therapy referrals as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop medications; flag drugs contributing to dizziness/sedation for review.
teaching: Report dizziness and use prescribed assistive devices consistently.
delegationScope: Environmental checks may be shared; medication/clinical risk interpretation requires licensed review.
examTrap: Teaching only 'move slowly' while ignoring sedating drugs and home hazards.
oneLinePearl: Falls are multifactorial, so prevention must be too.

title: Preventive Sexual Health: Normalize Risk-Based Screening
bottomLine: Sexual-health prevention should be confidential, nonjudgmental, and based on anatomy, practices, exposures, pregnancy potential, and current screening guidance rather than assumptions about identity.
recognize: Risk cannot be inferred from marital status, age alone, or sexual orientation labels.
priorities: Use respectful questions and preserve privacy according to law/policy.
assessMonitor: Clarify symptoms, partners/practices, barrier use, contraception, pregnancy risk, prior STIs, and immunization status as relevant.
interventions: Reinforce indicated screening, vaccination, safer-sex strategies, and referral.
medicationSafety: PrEP/PEP and STI therapies require specific prescribing and adherence plans.
teaching: Screening recommendations depend on current risk and guideline criteria.
delegationScope: History collection may be role-dependent; prescribing/diagnosis remain outside PN scope.
examTrap: Assuming no STI risk because the patient is married.
oneLinePearl: Ask about risk; do not guess it.

title: Skin Cancer Prevention: Teach Protection and Change Recognition
bottomLine: Preventive skin care includes reducing ultraviolet exposure and recognizing changing or suspicious lesions that need diagnostic evaluation.
recognize: New, changing, bleeding, nonhealing, or markedly asymmetric lesions warrant clinical review.
priorities: Reinforce sun protection and escalation of concerning changes.
assessMonitor: Ask about UV exposure, prior skin cancer, immunosuppression, and lesion changes.
interventions: Promote protective clothing/shade and sunscreen use according to current recommendations.
medicationSafety: Review photosensitizing medications when counseling about sun exposure.
teaching: Report evolving lesions rather than waiting for routine visits.
delegationScope: Teaching may be reinforced by PN/LVN; diagnosis remains provider responsibility.
examTrap: Reassuring a bleeding changing lesion because it is painless.
oneLinePearl: Changing skin lesions need evaluation, not watchful reassurance.

title: Preventive Medication Review: Reduce Avoidable Harm
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Preventive visits should include medication reconciliation, adherence barriers, OTC/supplement use, duplication, fall risk, and monitoring needs. The PN/LVN identifies problems and escalates for prescriber/pharmacy review rather than independently deprescribing.
recognize: Multiple prescribers, duplicate therapies, sedatives, anticholinergic burden, missed monitoring, and cost-related nonadherence increase risk.
priorities: Build the best possible medication list and flag discrepancies or adverse-effect concerns.
assessMonitor: Review names, doses, schedules, actual use, OTC/herbals, side effects, access, and required monitoring.
interventions: Reinforce the agreed regimen and facilitate pharmacist/prescriber review.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop chronic medications based on a preventive-risk screen.
teaching: Bring an updated medication list or actual containers to visits.
delegationScope: Medication-list collection may be assisted by trained staff; clinical reconciliation and escalation require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Deleting a medication from the list because the patient says they rarely take it without clarifying why.
oneLinePearl: Reconciliation asks what the patient actually takes, not only what was prescribed.
